title: Pagination, idempotency keys, API versioning and backward compatibility
scopeHtml: Scope: offset vs keyset pagination, sync APIs, idempotency key design, versioning strategies, backward-compatible change rules.

notes.title: Why pagination exists
notes.html:
Pagination returns a big list in small pages so responses stay fast, memory stays bounded, and the client shows data early. Without it, GET /orders for a user with 200,000 orders tries to load and ship hundreds of MB.

Three questions decide the design: how big is the dataset, can rows change while the user scrolls, and does the user need to jump to page 57?

Worked example. A feed item is 1.5 KB. A full 50,000-item list is 75 MB; at 1 Mbps that is 10 minutes. Pages of 20 are 30 KB, about 0.25 s. Choose limits like default 20, max 100 and reject larger.

Industry examples. Twitter/X and Instagram feeds use cursors. Stripe uses starting_after/ending_before object ids with limit (max 100) and has_more. GitHub uses page + per_page plus Link headers.

Everyday analogy. A book has chapters and pages; nobody reads 1,000 pages in one go.

Common interview traps.

  • Returning unbounded lists "because the data is small today".
  • No maximum limit, letting limit=1000000 through.

notes.title: Offset pagination
notes.html:
Offset pagination says "skip N rows, give me M": ?page=3&size=20 becomes LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40.

SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

Pros: trivial, supports "jump to page 57", gives total pages. Cons, both real:

  1. Slow on deep pages. The database still walks and discards the first N rows. OFFSET 1000000 reads a million rows to return 20. Latency grows linearly with page number: page 1 at 2 ms, page 50,000 maybe 800 ms or worse.
  2. Unstable. If a new row is inserted at the top while the user reads page 1, everything shifts by one: the last item of page 1 reappears as the first item of page 2 (duplicate). If a row is deleted, an item is skipped.

Also COUNT(*) for total pages is expensive on big tables (Postgres must scan; it has no cheap exact count). Many systems show "next" only, or an approximate count.

When it is fine. Admin screens, small tables (under about 10,000 rows), data that rarely changes, and when random page jump is needed.

Industry examples. Django REST Framework PageNumberPagination, Spring Data Pageable default to offset. Google Search shows "about 1,230,000 results" but caps real pages at around 30 to avoid deep offsets.

Everyday analogy. "Open the book and count 400 pages from the front each time" instead of using a bookmark.

Common interview traps.

  • Using offset for an infinite-scroll feed with live inserts.
  • Not mentioning the deep-offset cost in numbers.

notes.title: Keyset (cursor) pagination
notes.html:
Keyset pagination says "give me the 20 rows after THIS row", using the last row's sort key instead of a count.

-- first page
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- next page: pass the last row's (created_at, id)
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-11-09 10:00:00', 981234)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

Needs an index that matches the order: CREATE INDEX ON posts (created_at DESC, id DESC); Then every page is an index seek, about the same speed on page 1 and page 1,000,000.

Key points:

  • Sort key must be unique and stable: add a tiebreaker (id) since many rows share a timestamp; otherwise rows are skipped or repeated.
  • No random page jump and no easy "total".
  • Stable under inserts/deletes: you always continue after the last row you saw.
  • Opaque cursor: return next_cursor as a base64 (ideally signed/encrypted) blob like eyJ0IjoiMjAyNi0xMS0wOS4uLiIsImlkIjo5ODEyMzR9. Clients must not parse it, so you can change internals later. Include expiry and sort/filter fingerprint to reject mismatches.
{
  "data": [ { "id": 981233, "title": "..." } ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJ0IjoiMjAyNi0xMS0wOS4uLiIsImlkIjo5ODEyMzN9",
  "has_more": true
}

Worked example. Table of 100M rows. Offset page 100,000 (offset 2,000,000): scans 2M index entries, roughly 300 to 1,000 ms. Keyset: seeks to the position, reads 20 entries, about 1 to 3 ms. A feed endpoint at 20,000 QPS cannot afford the first.

Sorting by a non-unique or mutable column (e.g. score). Encode (score, id) in the cursor. If scores change between pages, a row can still jump; accept it or snapshot.

Industry examples. Facebook Graph API cursor pagination, Slack cursor, Twitter pagination_token, Stripe object-id cursors, DynamoDB LastEvaluatedKey, Elasticsearch search_after, Kafka consumer offsets are the same concept.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark: no matter what is added at the front of the book, you resume where you stopped.

Common interview traps.

  • Cursor on a non-unique column without a tiebreaker.
  • Cursor with OFFSET hidden inside it (defeats the purpose).
  • Letting clients forge cursors that read other users' data.

notes.title: Pagination response contract and choosing
notes.html:
State the contract so clients can be written once.

Style Request Response extras Jump to page Stable Speed deep
Offset page, size total, page yes no bad
Keyset after, limit next_cursor, has_more no yes great
Time-based since=timestamp latest timestamp no mostly great
Seek by id after_id last id no yes great

Also useful: a Link header (<...?after=abc>; rel="next"), and limit capped server-side.

Decision gravity. Switching offset to cursor later is a breaking change (clients assumed page). Start with cursor for anything user-facing that can grow past a few thousand rows; its cost now is small, the migration later is large. Offset is reversible-ish only for internal tools.

Sync API for mobile (offline-first). Use GET /changes?since=<server_version> returning created/updated/deleted records (with tombstones for deletes) so the Room database can sync incrementally. Use a monotonic server version, not client clocks.

Industry examples. Notion and Google Drive sync use change tokens. Google Calendar API syncToken.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper subscription: "send me everything since issue 1042", not "send me the entire archive each morning".

Common interview traps.

  • Offering both without saying when each is used.
  • Forgetting deleted rows in sync (client keeps stale data forever).

notes.title: Idempotency keys
notes.html:
An idempotency key lets a client safely retry a non-idempotent request (like "charge 500 rupees") without it being applied twice.

The client generates a unique key (UUIDv4) per logical operation and sends it in a header: Idempotency-Key: 7c1f.... The server stores the key with the result. A second request with the same key gets the stored response instead of re-executing.

Server algorithm:

  1. Receive request with key K.
  2. INSERT key K, status=IN_PROGRESS, request_hash with a unique constraint (atomic claim).
  3. If insert succeeded: do the work, save the response for K, mark DONE.
  4. If K exists and DONE: return the saved response (same status and body).
  5. If K exists and IN_PROGRESS: return 409 (or wait briefly); the first attempt is still running.
  6. If K exists but the request body hash differs: return 422/400 (key misuse).
  7. Expire keys after 24 hours (Stripe) or as needed.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key            text PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id        bigint NOT NULL,
  request_hash   bytea NOT NULL,
  status         text NOT NULL,          -- IN_PROGRESS | DONE
  response_code  int,
  response_body  jsonb,
  created_at     timestamptz DEFAULT now()
);
-- claim atomically
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, user_id, request_hash, status)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'IN_PROGRESS')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;   -- 0 rows inserted => already seen

The key insert and the business write should be in the same database transaction where possible; otherwise a crash between "charge done" and "response saved" leaves the state unknown. For external side effects (card network), pass the key downstream too (Stripe passes idempotency to its processors).

Worked example. User taps Pay; the response is lost in a tunnel; the app retries. Without a key: 2 charges of 1,999. With a key: attempt 2 finds K=DONE and returns the first receipt. At 1M payments/day and 0.5% retries, that avoids about 5,000 duplicate charges a day.

Where the key lives on Android. Generate the UUID when the user starts the action (button press / saved in a Room "pending operation" row), reuse it for all retries, even after process death. A new UUID per retry defeats the purpose.

Also dedupe on the consumer side. Message queues deliver at least once (Kafka, SQS). Consumers use an event id plus a processed-ids table, or natural idempotency (UPDATE ... SET status='PAID' rather than balance = balance + x).

Industry examples. Stripe (Idempotency-Key, 24h retention), PayPal (PayPal-Request-Id), Razorpay, Adyen, AWS (client tokens on RunInstances), Uber's payment flows.

Everyday analogy. A cheque number: the bank refuses to cash cheque #5543 twice, no matter how many times it is presented.

Common interview traps.

  • Generating the key on the server (useless: the client cannot reuse it).
  • Not binding the key to the request body or user.
  • Check-then-insert without a unique constraint (race lets both through).

notes.title: API versioning strategies
notes.html:
Versioning lets you change an API without breaking apps already installed. On mobile you cannot force-update everyone: 2-year-old app versions may still be 5 to 10% of traffic.

Strategy Example Pros Cons
URL path /v1/orders, /v2/orders Obvious, cacheable, easy routing URL changes, whole-API granularity
Header Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json Clean URLs Hidden, harder to test in a browser
Query param /orders?version=2 Easy Caches and routing messier
Date-based Stripe-Version: 2024-06-20 Fine-grained, per-account pinning Needs transformation layer
None (evolve only) Add fields only No duplication Needs discipline forever

Stripe's model: each account is pinned to the API version of its first call; behavior changes are written as small version "transformers" applied to a newest-internal response, so only one implementation exists but many shapes are served. Upgrades are opt-in.

Decision gravity. Maintaining N versions multiplies test and bug-fix cost. Prefer "evolve additively, version rarely". A new major version is a one-way door you will support for years; set a published deprecation policy (for example 12 months notice) when you launch.

Industry examples. Stripe (date versions), Twitter (v1.1 to v2 took years, v1.1 sunsets painful), GitHub (X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28), Google Maps (URL versions), Facebook Graph (v19.0, each lives about 2 years).

Everyday analogy. Keeping the old train line running while you open the new one; you only close it after everyone has moved.

Common interview traps.

  • Versioning for every tiny change.
  • Not mentioning telemetry on which version each client uses (needed to know when to sunset).

notes.title: Backward compatibility rules
notes.html:
A change is backward compatible if existing clients keep working without an update. Think about what old clients assume.

Safe (non-breaking):

  • Add a new optional request field or query parameter with a sensible default.
  • Add a new response field (clients must ignore unknown fields: the tolerant reader rule; configure Moshi/Gson/kotlinx-serialization ignoreUnknownKeys = true).
  • Add a new endpoint.
  • Add a new enum value, only if clients are told to handle unknown values.

Breaking:

  • Remove or rename a field or endpoint.
  • Change a type (int to string), unit (seconds to ms) or meaning.
  • Make an optional request field required.
  • Tighten validation (reject what used to pass).
  • Change error codes/shapes that clients branch on.
  • Change default sort order or page size.
  • Turn a non-null into nullable (crashes Kotlin non-null models).

Techniques:

  • Expand and contract (parallel change): add the new field, keep the old, migrate clients, remove old later. Same for DB schema (add column, backfill, switch reads, drop).
  • Feature flags and server-driven defaults.
  • Deprecation signals: Deprecation: true and Sunset: <date> headers (RFC 8594 for Sunset), docs, and log which clients still call it.
  • Force-upgrade gate: the API returns 426 Upgrade Required or an app-config min_supported_version so the app shows an update screen as a last resort.
  • Contract tests (Pact) and OpenAPI diff in CI (for example oasdiff) to block breaking changes automatically.
// Tolerant reader on Android
val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; coerceInputValues = true }

@Serializable
data class Order(val id: String, val status: String = "UNKNOWN") // default for missing/new

Worked example. Rename price (rupees, float) to amount_minor (paise, int). Wrong: rename in place, old apps show prices of 0. Right: ship both for 2 releases, watch usage of apps still reading price fall to under 1%, then remove with a 90-day sunset notice.

Industry examples. Protobuf's design is built for this (field numbers, unknown fields preserved). Google's AIP guidelines list breaking-change rules. Slack and Stripe publish changelogs with explicit "backwards-compatible changes" lists.

Everyday analogy. Changing a plug shape: first ship adapters that fit both, then retire the old plug.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "adding a field is always safe" (strict deserializers, or enums with exhaustive when, can crash).
  • Deploying server first vs app first without an order plan: for additive changes, deploy the server first; for removals, remove the usage in clients first.
  • Forgetting that old messages already stored in queues/DB still have the old format.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Pagination: always cap limit. Offset is simple but slow deep and unstable under inserts; keyset/cursor is fast and stable but cannot jump to a page. Use opaque, signed cursors with a unique tiebreaker and a matching index.
  • For offline sync use changes?since=version with tombstones.
  • Idempotency keys: client-generated per logical operation, stored with a unique constraint, same transaction as the work, return the saved response on retry, 409 while in progress, expire after about 24 h. Consumers of queues dedupe too.
  • Versioning: prefer additive evolution; when needed use URL (/v1) or date headers; every version is a long-term cost, so publish a deprecation policy and measure usage.
  • Backward compatibility: tolerant readers, expand and contract, never rename/remove/retype in place, deprecation headers, CI breaking-change checks, and a min-version force-upgrade as the last resort.

questions.promptHtml: What are the problems with offset pagination and what does keyset pagination do differently?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pagination is on nearly every list API; deep-page cost and instability are classic production issues.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Offset says "skip N rows, give M", so OFFSET 1000000 makes the database walk and discard a million rows; latency grows with page number. It is also unstable: an insert at the top shifts everything and I see a duplicate or miss a row. Keyset says "give me rows after this last key", using an index seek, so every page costs the same and it is stable under inserts. The trade-off is no jump to page 57 and no cheap total.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
-- offset
SELECT id, title FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;
-- keyset (needs index on (created_at DESC, id DESC))
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-11-09 10:00:00', 981234)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

Rough numbers on 100M rows: offset 2,000,000 scans 2M index entries, 300 to 1,000 ms; keyset 1 to 3 ms. Offset is fine for admin screens, small tables (under about 10,000 rows) and when users must jump to a page. COUNT(*) for total pages is expensive on large tables.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Offset on an infinite-scroll feed with live inserts.
  • No cap on limit.
  • Hiding an OFFSET inside a "cursor".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a tiebreaker like id? -> Many rows share a timestamp; without a unique key rows are skipped or repeated.
  2. How do you show total pages? -> Approximate count or "next" only.
  3. What if the sort field is mutable (score)? -> Encode (score, id); a row may still jump, accept it or snapshot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "offset is slow". Senior gives the scan math, the instability case and when offset is still right.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed endpoint at 20K QPS could not afford deep offsets; moving to keyset dropped DB CPU sharply.

questions.promptHtml: What is an idempotency key and how does the server implement it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Payment and order APIs must survive client retries; it checks that you can design dedupe correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client generates a unique key per logical operation, such as a UUID created when the user taps Pay, and sends it as Idempotency-Key. The server atomically inserts the key with a unique constraint, does the work once, stores the response, and on any retry with the same key returns the stored response. A key seen while still in progress gets 409, and the same key with a different body is rejected.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, user_id, request_hash, status)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'IN_PROGRESS')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;     -- 0 rows => already seen

Steps: claim -> do work -> save response (code, body) -> mark DONE. Put the claim and the business write in one DB transaction where possible. Expire keys after about 24 hours (Stripe's period). On Android, generate the UUID when the action starts, persist it in a Room "pending operation" row, and reuse it for every retry, even after process death.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Server-generated keys (the client cannot reuse them).
  • Check-then-insert without a unique constraint (race).
  • Not binding the key to the user and request body.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Same key, different body? -> 422/400, key misuse.
  2. Request still running? -> 409 or wait briefly.
  3. Queue consumers? -> At-least-once delivery, so dedupe by event id in a processed-ids table.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "store the key". Senior covers atomic claim, same-transaction writes, in-progress state, expiry, and client-side persistence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A response lost in a tunnel caused double charges until keys were added.

questions.promptHtml: Which API changes are backward compatible and which are breaking? Does "adding a field is always safe" hold?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you can change a live API without breaking installed apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Adding an optional request field, a new response field or a new endpoint is usually safe, provided clients are tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, unit or meaning, making an optional field required, tightening validation, changing error codes, default sort or page size, or making a non-null field nullable are breaking. "Adding is always safe" is false: strict deserializers and exhaustive enum switches can crash.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Safe:     new optional param, new response field, new endpoint, new enum value (if clients tolerate)
Breaking: remove/rename, type or unit change, required-ization, stricter validation,
          error shape change, default sort/page size change, non-null -> nullable

Technique: expand and contract. Add the new field, keep the old, migrate clients, watch usage, remove later. Signals: Deprecation: true, Sunset: <date>. Last resort: 426 Upgrade Required or a min_supported_version.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; coerceInputValues = true }

@Serializable
data class Order(val id: String, val status: String = "UNKNOWN")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Renaming a field because it is nicer.
  • Forgetting that messages already in queues or DB use the old format.
  • Deploying removals server-first (remove client usage first).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Deploy order for additive change? -> Server first.
  2. How to catch breaks in CI? -> OpenAPI diff (oasdiff), contract tests (Pact).
  3. Enums? -> Tell clients to handle unknown values with a default.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists breaking changes. Senior adds tolerant reader, expand-contract, telemetry and CI enforcement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A renamed price field showed zero prices in old app versions for hours.

questions.contextHtml:
A back-office orders export UI paginates with LIMIT 50 OFFSET (page-1)*50 on a 120M-row table. Ops scripts crawl all pages. DB shows:

GET /orders?page=1       18 ms
GET /orders?page=2000    210 ms
GET /orders?page=40000   2.9 s     (OFFSET 1,999,950)
Primary CPU 85%, replica lag 12 s, 6 concurrent crawlers
EXPLAIN: Index Scan on orders_created_idx  rows=2000000 (discarded) ... Limit
questions.promptHtml: Why does latency grow and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more indexes." An index already exists; the scan of skipped rows is inherent to OFFSET.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does anyone need to jump to arbitrary pages? Are the crawlers exports (full scan) or users? Is data changing while they crawl?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle the crawlers, route them to a replica, cap page at a sane depth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Deep OFFSET reads and discards rows linearly; concurrent crawlers amplify; replica lag from CPU pressure. Red herring: the index is present and used.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) at several offsets, slow-query log by offset size.
  5. Root cause: Cost is O(offset) per request, so a full crawl is O(N^2/pageSize).
  6. Fix: Keyset WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50, index (created_at DESC, id DESC); opaque cursor; bulk export via a separate async job reading in id ranges.
  7. Prevention: Maximum limit and depth, query-time alerts, cursor by default for tables over about 10K rows.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keyset loses page jumps (provide search/filter and date range); I would not keep page= as the public contract.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Support insists on page numbers -> Keep offset only for small filtered result sets with a hard cap.
  • Total count? -> Approximate or cached count.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly crawler on deep offsets pushed a primary to saturation; a cursor and a bulk-export job fixed it permanently.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds indexes.
  • Hire: keyset with matching index.
  • Strong hire: explains O(N^2) crawl, mitigation order, export job and contract change.

questions.contextHtml:
A feed API uses a keyset cursor on created_at only. Users report duplicates and "missing posts" in infinite scroll. Import jobs insert hundreds of posts with the same timestamp.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
List<Post> next(Instant after, int limit) {
    return jdbc.query(
      "SELECT * FROM posts WHERE created_at < ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?",
      mapper, after, limit);
}
// cursor = base64(created_at of last row), unsigned
fun next(after: Instant, limit: Int): List<Post> = jdbc.query(
    "SELECT * FROM posts WHERE created_at < ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?",
    mapper, after, limit)
// cursor = base64(created_at of last row), unsigned
page 1 ends at created_at = 10:00:00.000 (rows A,B,C share it; only A fits on page 1)
page 2: WHERE created_at < 10:00:00.000  -> B and C are never shown
limit param: no maximum ; cursor: plain base64

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It works for most users." Misses skipped rows and the forged-cursor risk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is created_at unique? Can clients see other users' posts via a forged cursor? Is the sort order fixed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap limit and treat the cursor as opaque.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Non-unique sort key skips rows (with <= instead you would duplicate them). No tiebreaker. Unsigned cursor can be tampered with. No limit cap.
  4. How I'd verify each: Insert 5 rows with identical timestamps and page with limit 2; decode the cursor and alter it.
  5. Root cause: Key is not a total order, and the cursor trusts the client.
  6. Fix: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC and WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?); index (created_at DESC, id DESC); cursor = signed (HMAC) or encrypted blob with sort key, filter hash and expiry; limit default 20, max 100; return has_more.
  7. Prevention: Test with duplicate timestamps, property test that paging yields every row exactly once.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Signing costs little; encryption hides internals. I would not use OFFSET inside the cursor.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sort by a changing score -> Cursor (score, id); a row may move between pages, document it or snapshot.
  • Cursor reuse across filters? -> Include a filter hash and reject mismatches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Bulk-imported rows with identical timestamps made a feed silently drop content for a few users for months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: does not see the bug.
  • Hire: adds id tiebreaker and tuple comparison.
  • Strong hire: signed opaque cursor, limit cap, index and a property test.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments endpoint claims idempotency. Production sees occasional double charges when the Android app taps twice. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@PostMapping("/payments")
public Response pay(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key, @RequestBody PayReq r) {
    var saved = keyRepo.find(key);          // 1) check
    if (saved != null) return saved.response();
    var resp = gateway.charge(r);           // 2) side effect
    keyRepo.save(key, resp);                // 3) store
    return resp;
}
@PostMapping("/payments")
fun pay(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") key: String, @RequestBody r: PayReq): Response {
    keyRepo.find(key)?.let { return it.response }   // check
    val resp = gateway.charge(r)                    // side effect
    keyRepo.save(key, resp)                         // store
    return resp
}
10:01:02.100 key=abc find -> null   (thread 1)
10:01:02.104 key=abc find -> null   (thread 2)
10:01:02.900 charge OK x2           duplicate
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized." That only protects one JVM instance; there are many pods.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the table have a unique constraint? Is it multi-instance? Does the gateway support its own idempotency key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a UNIQUE constraint on the key and disable double-tap in the UI.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-act race across two requests; no atomic claim; crash between charge and save leaves unknown state. Red herring: duplicated button taps are not the cause, just the trigger.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fire two parallel requests with the same key in a test; reconcile charges vs key rows.
  5. Root cause: Reading before writing is not atomic.
  6. Fix: Atomically claim with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (status IN_PROGRESS, request hash); if 0 rows, return the stored response or 409 if still in progress; do the work, store the response, mark DONE, in one transaction where possible. Pass the same key to the payment provider so an external retry is safe too.
  7. Prevention: Concurrency test in CI, reconciliation job, alert on duplicate charges.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A distributed lock adds failure modes; the DB unique constraint is simpler. I would not generate keys server-side.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Request body differs for the same key -> 422, key misuse.
  • Crash after charge but before saving -> Provider-side key or a reconciliation job resolves the unknown state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fintech's "idempotent" endpoint double-charged for a few hundred customers during a deploy because two pods raced on the same key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: uses synchronized.
  • Hire: unique constraint with atomic insert.
  • Strong hire: in-progress state, hash binding, provider key and reconciliation.

questions.promptHtml: What are the main API versioning strategies, and how would you choose for a mobile-first public API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mobile clients cannot be force-updated, so versioning is a long-term cost decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: URL path (/v1), header/media type, query parameter, date-based (Stripe's account-pinned version) or none with strictly additive evolution. For a mobile-first API I prefer additive evolution as the default and a URL major version only for real breaks, because old app versions can stay at 5 to 10% of traffic for years. Whatever I choose, I publish a deprecation policy and measure usage per version.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
URL path   /v1/orders                 obvious, cacheable, whole-API granularity
Header     Accept: ...v2+json         clean URLs, hidden, harder to test
Query      /orders?version=2          easy, messy caching
Date       Stripe-Version: 2024-06-20 fine-grained, needs a transform layer
None       additive only              no duplication, needs permanent discipline

Route by version at a gateway, share one core, and put adapters in front (v1 adapter, v2 adapter). Each live version multiplies test and bug-fix cost. A new major version is a one-way door you support for years.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Versioning every small change.
  • No telemetry on which version each client uses.
  • Forking the codebase per version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How long do you support old versions? -> A published window (for example 12 to 24 months), extended by usage data.
  2. How do you retire? -> Deprecation/Sunset headers, outreach, final 426 or 410.
  3. Why does date-based versioning work for Stripe? -> A transformer layer maps one internal shape to many versions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks /v1. Senior weighs cost per version, forced-update ability, telemetry and the one-way nature.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A v1 kept alive for years because nobody knew which clients still used it.

questions.contextHtml: The PM says: "Make the notes app work offline and keep phones in sync." Server has 2M users, 300 notes each on average, phones come online irregularly. Today the app calls GET /notes?page=N and replaces the local Room table with everything.
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the API, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Poll the full list every minute." Heavy and it never learns about deletions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can two devices edit the same note (conflict rule)? How long can a phone be offline? Do we need delete propagation? Is data end-to-end encrypted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop full replace; compress and add ETag to the current endpoint while the new design ships.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: An incremental change feed handles most cases; the main risks are deletes (tombstones), conflicts and a client that is offline longer than server retention.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with two devices; test an offline window longer than tombstone retention.
  5. Root cause (of the pain): The contract has no notion of "what changed since".
  6. Fix: GET /changes?since=<server_version>&limit=200 returning created, updated and deleted items (tombstones) with a new monotonic next_version and has_more; the client stores the version, applies changes in a transaction, and pushes local changes with If-Match or per-item version and idempotency keys. If since is older than retention, reply 410 Gone with a hint to do a full resync via cursor pagination.
  7. Prevention: Tests with long offline, conflict simulation, metrics on resync rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Tombstones cost storage (purge after a retention window); I would not use wall-clock timestamps as the version because clocks skew, use a server-side monotonic version.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two devices edit the same note -> Last-writer-wins per field or a merge dialog, decided up front.
  • Millions of changes after a long offline -> Cap with resync via snapshot.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sync built on client timestamps lost edits when a phone clock was wrong by a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: full poll.
  • Hire: since-version change feed with deletes.
  • Strong hire: asks about conflicts and offline window, tombstone retention, 410 resync and idempotent pushes.

questions.contextHtml:
Payments API with idempotency keys, 1M payments/day. After a database failover at 03:12 support sees customers with a pending payment that never resolves:

idempotency_keys: key=k91 status=IN_PROGRESS created_at=03:12:04   (rows stuck: 212)
provider ledger:  charge for k91 SUCCEEDED
client retries:   POST /payments key=k91  -> 409 "request in progress"  (for 40 minutes)

The service crashed after the provider call and before saving the response.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is going on, how you unstick users now and how you design it to be safe.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete the stuck keys so retries run again." That can charge a second time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider accept our key and return the original result on retry? Can we query the provider by reference? What is the retry window on clients?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not delete rows. For the 212 stuck keys, look up each charge at the provider by the key/reference and complete the row with the true outcome.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Crash between the external side effect and recording the result (the unavoidable gap); no timeout/recovery for IN_PROGRESS; the provider call did not use our key. Red herring: the failover itself, which only caused the crash.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare key rows to provider records, check logs around 03:12:04.
  5. Root cause: An external side effect cannot join our DB transaction, and IN_PROGRESS rows had no owner or expiry.
  6. Fix: Pass the same idempotency key to the provider so a re-execution is safe; store a lease (locked_until) on IN_PROGRESS; a recovery worker re-drives expired rows by asking the provider for state; return 409 with Retry-After while running; write intent first, then side effect, then result (outbox pattern).
  7. Prevention: Alert on IN_PROGRESS older than N minutes, nightly reconciliation against the provider ledger, chaos test killing the process mid-call.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Exactly-once does not exist across systems; the design is at-least-once plus idempotency. I would not hold a DB transaction open across a network call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider has no idempotency support -> Use its lookup by merchant reference and reconcile before retrying.
  • Key expiry vs long retries? -> Keep keys longer than any client retry horizon (24 h typical).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a failover a recovery job that "retried stuck rows" double-charged customers because it did not ask the provider first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes keys.
  • Hire: reconciles with the provider, adds lease/recovery.
  • Strong hire: outbox/intent pattern, provider key, reconciliation, alerts and honest trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: Orders API returns price as float rupees (for example 199.5). Finance wants integer paise as amount_minor after a rounding discrepancy of 0.01 on 0.3% of invoices. Usage by app version in the last 7 days: v7 (current) 61%, v6 24%, v5 11%, older 4%. Server and apps deploy independently; 2M DAU.
questions.promptHtml: Give the migration plan with sequencing and exit criteria.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rename the field and release a new app." Old apps would show zero prices.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do queues or caches store old-format messages? Which partners read price? Can we force update older than v5? What is the deadline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None for users; fix the rounding on the server using integer math from the source of truth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The risk is old apps and stored messages, not the server code; the long tail (4% old) defines the end date.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log app version on every call, count responses where the client sends price readers, check consumers.
  5. Root cause: Wrong representation (float) shipped in the contract.
  6. Fix: Expand and contract. Step 1: server returns both price (rounded from the integer) and amount_minor; tolerant-reader enabled. Step 2: app v8 reads amount_minor. Step 3: watch usage of apps reading price; set Deprecation/Sunset on the field in docs and changelog. Step 4: when traffic from old versions is under 1%, notify, then show a min-version update gate for the rest. Step 5: stop sending price. Same for DB and events: dual-write then drop.
  7. Prevention: oasdiff in CI, contract tests, rule "never retype in place".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Extra payload and a duplicate field for months; I would not remove price on a date chosen without usage data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old events in Kafka have price -> Consumers accept both until the topic retention passes.
  • Partner cannot change -> Frozen adapter with a sunset date in the contract.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An in-place rename passed all server tests and showed zero prices to 5% of users on old builds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: renames in place.
  • Hire: ships both fields, migrates clients, then removes.
  • Strong hire: exit criteria from telemetry, force-upgrade gate, event/DB handling and CI protection.

questions.contextHtml: Public API GET /transactions?page=N&size=50 serves 12K rps on a 2B-row table. Traffic will grow 10x after a partner launch. Today: p99 450 ms; the DB spends 70% of time on offsets over 10,000. 200 partners and 3 app versions use page. Partners need an end date for any change.
questions.promptHtml: How do you move to cursor pagination without breaking clients, and what do you size?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add read replicas." Capacity multiplies cost for an inherently linear scan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of requests go above page 100? Do partners crawl everything or show lists? Is the sort order fixed or user-chosen? Do they rely on total?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap page x size at a limit (say 10,000 offset) returning an error with guidance; route deep traffic to a replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Few clients cause deep scans (crawlers); most use pages 1 to 5; some partners rely on total.
  4. How I'd verify each: Histogram of page depth, top callers by depth.
  5. Root cause: Offset cost grows linearly with depth, 10x traffic multiplies a bad tail.
  6. Fix: Add after/next_cursor (opaque, signed, with sort and filter hash) alongside page; response includes next_cursor and has_more from day one; index (account_id, created_at DESC, id DESC); document that page is deprecated with Sunset; cap offset; offer /exports for bulk reads. Math: at 120K rps a cursor seek of about 2 ms uses roughly 240 DB-seconds per second of work spread across the fleet; offset above 10,000 costs 10 to 100x more per request.
  7. Prevention: Default new list endpoints to cursors, cap limit, load test deep pages.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Loses random page access and total; provide approximate counts via a separate endpoint. I would not remove page without partner notice and usage data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cursor forged to read another tenant -> Bind account id in the signed payload.
  • Partners sort by amount -> Cursor holds (amount, id), index per supported sort.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single partner crawling to page 400,000 cost more DB time than all other users combined; a cursor and export endpoint removed the problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: replicas only.
  • Hire: cursor added next to page with deprecation.
  • Strong hire: measures depth, caps, signed cursors, index design, bulk export and a sunset plan.

questions.contextHtml:
You run /v1 through /v4 of a public API. Cost review:

version  traffic  clients               eng cost/quarter
v1       0.8%     2 partners, old apps  ~3 eng-weeks (security patches, tests)
v2       3%       old apps              ~2 eng-weeks
v3       41%      current apps          shared core
v4       55%      new apps              shared core
v1 hit by a vulnerability scanner; fix needed in v1 and v2 handlers

Leadership asks: "Kill v1 and v2 next month?"
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide and execute? What is the gravity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, only 4% of traffic." Ignores who the 4% are (revenue) and the notice owed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who are the v1 partners and what revenue do they carry? What does the contract/deprecation policy promise? Can the old apps be force-updated? What is the real per-version maintenance cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Patch the vulnerability in v1 and v2 now; maintenance of a security hole is not optional while they run.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The 0.8% may be a high-value partner; v2 traffic may be a long tail of old apps that a gate can retire; the code cost may shrink by turning v1/v2 into thin adapters over v4.
  4. How I'd verify each: Traffic by client and revenue, adapter feasibility, contract terms.
  5. Root cause: Versions were added without a published sunset schedule or telemetry.
  6. Fix and decision: Sunset is a one-way door for those clients. Publish a timeline (for example 6 months notice), send Deprecation and Sunset headers, email partners directly, add an in-app update prompt for v2 then a min-version gate, provide a migration guide, and consider a paid/extended support arrangement for the v1 partners. Re-implement v1/v2 as adapters over the v4 core to cut cost meanwhile. Brownout tests (short planned outages) before the final cut.
  7. Prevention: A written policy ("each major version supported 24 months after the next one ships"), per-client dashboards from day one.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keeping old versions costs engineering time and security surface; killing them early costs trust and revenue. I would not announce a date before checking contract terms.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner refuses to migrate -> Escalate commercially; offer frozen adapter at a price.
  • Date-based versioning instead? -> Fewer majors, but needs the transformer layer; consider for v5.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scanner finding in an "unused" old version turned into a fire drill because nobody owned its code or its few remaining callers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: kills by traffic share alone.
  • Hire: policy, notice, headers and telemetry.
  • Strong hire: weighs revenue and contracts, patches now, adapters, brownouts and a standing policy.
